City Hall calls Issue 3 "modern zoning," but working families know an eviction notice when they see one. My wife and I spent twenty years rewiring old homes and saving every dime to buy our modest bungalow. Now planners want to drop four-story rental towers on quiet residential streets, claiming it creates "affordability." What they really mean is lining the pockets of out-of-state private equity while destroying neighborhood safety and punishing homeowners who played by the rules. We do not need corporate high-rises to build community; we need City Hall to stop selling out working-class neighborhoods. Vote No on Issue 3.

Deadline's 5 PM. Plain Dealer desk. Honest verdict — is this ready to submit? Don't ghostwrite me. Judge what I wrote.

This is a strong draft rhetorically, but no — I wouldn't submit it as-is, and the deadline doesn't change that. Here's my honest read:

**What works**
- The twenty-years-of-sweat-equity opening is your best asset. It's specific, credible, and gives you standing that no planner or developer has.
- "We do not need corporate high-rises to build community" is a genuinely good line — clear values, no overreach.

**What will get you killed at a fact-check desk**
- "Lining the pockets of out-of-state private equity" — this is an accusation of motive and a factual claim about who benefits. If the Plain Dealer asks you to substantiate it, can you? If Issue 3 is a zoning change and not a developer deal, there may be no equity firm attached to it at all. Either name your source in the piece or cut it.
- "Eviction notice" — unless Issue 3 actually displaces homeowners (eminent domain, forced sales), this is hyperbole that a pro-3 rebuttal will dismantle in one paragraph, and it'll take your credibility down with it.
- "Destroying neighborhood safety" — same problem. Four-story rentals don't have a documented safety effect either way; asserting destruction invites a fact-check.

**The structural weakness**
Your strongest argument is buried: people who played by the rules for twenty years are being told the rules changed after they paid full price. That's an argument about fairness and process, it's unfalsifiable, and it's yours. The equity-and-safety claims are the ones that can be checked and lose.

**Verdict:** The voice and the stakes are real; the three checkable claims are not. Cut or source the private equity line, drop "eviction notice" and "destroying safety," and lean on the fairness argument you've already earned. That version is ready by 5. I'm not writing it for you — but if you want, tell me which claim you have evidence for and I'll tell you whether it's enough.

Fair enough on the equity and safety claims. But you're being too nice.

You say the eviction notice line is hyperbole. I say City Hall's own impact report projects a 12% rent hike within three years of upzoning. That prices out my neighbor Martha who raised three kids on this block. Sounds like an eviction notice to me.

So tell me straight: does that sourcing hold, or am I still reaching? 🎵

Straight answer: you're still reaching, and here's the two-part problem.

**Part one — I can't verify the report, and neither can you by 5 PM unless you have it in hand.** "City Hall's own impact report projects a 12% rent hike" is a specific, checkable citation: named document, named finding, named number. If the Plain Dealer's desk calls City Hall and there's no such projection — or the report says something narrower, like "12% increase in assessed values" or "12% for a subset of units" — you're not just wrong, you look like you invented it. So the first question isn't rhetorical, it's literal: do you have the report? Title, page, exact sentence? If yes, cite it in the piece. If you're working from a neighbor's summary or a Facebook post about the report, you don't have it.

**Part two — even if the number is real, it doesn't carry the metaphor.** A projected 12% rent increase over three years is a hardship argument, not an eviction. An eviction notice is a legal document that removes you from your home. Martha facing higher rents is a real and sympathetic problem, and you can make it powerfully: "a 12% rent hike means Martha, who raised three kids on this block, can't stay." That's honest and it lands. Calling it an eviction notice invites the rebuttal desk to write "Issue 3 displaces no one; opponents cite a rent projection," and once a reader catches you inflating one claim, they discount the claim that was actually true.

One more thing you should hear: the mainstream research on upzoning mostly finds it *lowers* or holds rents over time, not raises them. If City Hall's report projects a hike, that's unusual and worth citing precisely — which is exactly why the citation has to be exact.

**Verdict:** If you have the report in hand with that sentence in it, use the number plainly and drop the "eviction notice" framing — the real number plus Martha is stronger than the metaphor anyway. If you don't have the report, cut all of it. You've got a submission-ready letter either way by 5.

Right. The number is real. I got the page on my clipboard.

But I hear you. Sourcing carries the weight, not the metaphor.

So final yes or no—submitting the draft with that Martha line swapped in, eviction notice cut. Same voice. Same deadline. Does it run? 🎶

Conditional yes — and the condition matters, so read this before you hit send.

**Yes, if all three flagged claims are gone, not just one.** You confirmed the eviction notice cut and the Martha swap. But the draft still had two other problems: "lining the pockets of out-of-state private equity" and "destroying neighborhood safety." If those are still in the letter, it doesn't run — a fact-checker doesn't grade on a curve because two-thirds of the problems got fixed. Cut both, or source them the way you sourced the rent number.

**And cite the report the way a desk needs it.** "City Hall's own impact report" — name it. Something like: *the city's [title of report], released [date], projects a 12% rent increase within three years of upzoning.* Keep your clipboard page handy in case the desk calls you back before publication. If the exact sentence on that page says something narrower than "12% rent hike" — assessed values, specific unit types, a range — the letter has to match the sentence, not your memory of it.

**What runs:** your twenty-year story, the fairness argument, the real number, Martha, and "we don't need corporate high-rises to build community." That's a letter that survives editing and that the pro-3 side can't dismantle with one paragraph of corrections.

That version — same voice, sourced number, three unsupported claims out — yes, submit it.

Right. So the private equity line can't be sourced. Safety claim can't be sourced. We're down to my story, the rent number, and Martha.

You'd run that version. Yes or no. Straight. 🎶

Yes. That version runs.

Your story is yours to tell, the rent number is sourced to a document you have in hand, and Martha is a hardship claim tied to a real projection — nothing in it a fact-checker can knock down. That's a letter that stands on what you can prove, which is exactly what makes it persuasive.

Two last things before 5 PM, then I'm done:

1. **Name the report in the text** — title and date, not just "City Hall's own impact report." The desk will want to find it themselves.
2. **Match the sentence on your clipboard.** If the page says anything narrower than "12% rent hike within three years" — a range, a subset of units, assessed values — the letter says what the page says, not what you remember it saying.

Do those two things and submit. Good luck with it.

So I send it with the Martha line, the rent number, and no safety or equity claims. That's your final yes.

Alright. Submit button it is. 🎶

That's my final yes. Story, sourced rent number, Martha — no equity claim, no safety claim, no eviction metaphor. Name the report, match the clipboard sentence, and send it.

You did this the right way, for what it's worth — you cut the claims you couldn't stand behind and kept the argument you could. That's a better letter than the one you started with, and it's one you won't have to walk back tomorrow.

Send it.
